Benevolence of God
beh-NEV-oh-lens uv god
noun phrase (a divine attribute)
From the Latin bene (well) and velle (to wish); the goodness of God considered as His good-will toward His creatures, doing them good.

📖 Biblical Definition

The benevolence of God is the goodness of God considered as His good-will toward His creatures—His disposition to do them good and the kindness by which He actually does it. It is an aspect of the divine goodness, that perfection by which God is in Himself infinitely good and is the fountain of all good to His works. “The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works,” says the Psalmist; “the LORD is good; his mercy is everlasting.” This benevolence appears in two ranges. There is a general benevolence—often called common grace—by which God does good to all without distinction: He maketh His sun to rise on the evil and on the good, sendeth rain on the just and the unjust, fills men's hearts with food and gladness, and gives every good and perfect gift from above, with whom is no variableness. And there is His special, saving benevolence toward His elect, the everlasting love by which He chose, redeemed, and will glorify His people. The dictionary marks the benevolence of God against two errors. The first, a sentimental universalism, so magnifies God's general goodness as to deny His justice, holiness, and wrath—making benevolence the only attribute and concluding that He will save all and punish none. But the same God who is good to all is also just, and His benevolence does not cancel His holiness. The second error so fears that sentimentality that it underplays God's genuine kindness even to the wicked and His tender mercy to His own. The dictionary holds the balance Scripture holds: God is truly and abundantly good, the giver of every good gift, tender in mercy over all His works—and that goodness is never severed from His justice, but crowned, for the elect, in the unspeakable gift of His Son.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The goodness of God as His good-will toward His creatures (Psalm 145:9; Psalm 100:5); seen in general benevolence (common grace) to all and special saving love to the elect—abundant yet never severed from His justice and holiness.

expand to see more

BENEVOLENCE OF GOD, noun phrase. [Latin bene velle, to wish well.] God's good-will toward His creatures, doing them good.

“The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works” (Psalm 145:9).

General benevolence (common grace): sun and rain on just and unjust (Matthew 5:45).

Special saving benevolence: His everlasting love toward the elect.

Abundant goodness, never severed from His justice and holiness.

📖 Key Scripture

Ps 145:9 — "The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works."

Mt 5:45 — "That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust."

Ps 100:5 — "For the LORD is good; his mercy is everlasting; and his truth endureth to all generations."

Jas 1:17 — "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Sentimental universalism magnifies God's benevolence until it cancels His justice and wrath; the opposite error underplays His genuine kindness to the wicked and tender mercy to His own.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the goodness of God held together with His justice. The first corruption is a sentimental universalism that so magnifies the divine benevolence as to make it the only attribute—concluding that a good God will save all and punish none, that love cancels wrath, and that holiness must yield to kindness. The dictionary answers that the same God who is good to all is also just, holy, and a consuming fire; His benevolence is real and abundant but never severed from His other perfections, for in the simplicity of God all His attributes are one. A goodness that excludes justice is not the goodness of the God of Scripture.

The opposite error, in dread of sentimentality, so stresses God's wrath and justice that it underplays His genuine kindness—forgetting that He is good to all, sends rain on the unjust, fills men with food and gladness, and is tender in mercy over all His works, and that toward His own His benevolence rises to the unspeakable gift of His Son. The dictionary holds the balance Scripture holds: God is truly, abundantly, and tenderly good, the fountain and giver of every good and perfect gift; and that goodness, far from cancelling His justice, is crowned for the elect in the cross, where benevolence and justice meet and kiss.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Latin bene (well) and velle (to wish); an aspect of the divine goodness (Hebrew tov; Greek agathosune), God's good-will toward His creatures.

expand to see more

Bene velle, Latin, “to wish well,” the root of “benevolence.”

Tov, Hebrew, good; “the LORD is good to all” (Psalm 145:9).

Agathosune, Greek, goodness, a fruit of the Spirit and a perfection of God.

General benevolence (common grace) toward all; special benevolence toward the elect.

Held together with God's justice and holiness in the simplicity of His being.

Usage

"The teacher preached the benevolence of God, good to all, yet never severed from His justice."

"He answered the universalist that a goodness which cancels wrath is not the God of Scripture."

"She gave thanks for every good gift from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness."
